1.title: A tent no one could enter lightly
1.context: Exodus ends with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle so completely that Moses cannot enter it. Leviticus opens with God calling to Moses from inside that tent.
1.question: When have you felt both drawn toward God and aware that you could not approach Him carelessly?

1.title: The pattern of the burnt offering
1.context: The burnt offering was wholly burned on the altar. The offerer laid a hand on the animal's head, identifying with it before it was offered.
1.question: What does it mean to you that approaching God began with a gift placed entirely in His hands?

1.title: Bread, oil, and the salt of the covenant
1.context: The grain offering came from ordinary food: flour, oil, and frankincense. Salt was never to be missing from it, and the text calls it the salt of the covenant.
1.question: Where in your ordinary work or kitchen life might an offering be hiding?

1.title: A shared table with God
1.context: Unlike the burnt offering, the peace offering was eaten. God received the fat, the priests received a portion, and the offerer's household shared the meal.
1.question: What changes when worship is pictured as a meal shared rather than a debt paid?

1.title: When sin is unintentional
1.context: Chapter 4 addresses sins committed unintentionally, including sins the whole congregation did not know it had committed. The scale of the offering matches the reach of the sin.
1.question: How do you respond when you discover a wrong you did without realizing it?

1.title: Confession, and an offering for the poor
1.context: The sin offering's scale slides with a person's means, down to two birds, and finally to a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for the one who could afford nothing with blood in it.
1.question: What does the flour offering say about who this worship was designed to include?

1.title: Restitution first, then the ram
1.context: The guilt offering dealt with wrongs that could be measured. Where a neighbor had been defrauded, the debt was repaid in full, with a fifth added, before the ram was brought to the priest.
1.question: When an apology needs more than words, what does making it right look like in your life?

1.title: The fire that must not go out
1.context: The last two chapters of this section speak to the priests rather than the whole people. The altar fire was to be kept burning continually, tended every morning.
1.question: What daily practices keep something important from going out in your life?

1.title: The way in, waiting for priests
1.context: The section closes with a summary spoken on Mount Sinai. The laws name Aaron and his sons throughout, but no priest has yet been ordained to carry them out.
1.question: Where are you waiting for preparation to finish before a responsibility can begin?

2.title: The whole congregation assembled
2.context: Ordination in Israel was public. The whole congregation was gathered at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to watch Aaron and his sons set apart.
2.question: What is gained when a beginning is witnessed by a whole community rather than done in private?

2.title: Washed, robed, and anointed
2.context: Aaron's garments are put on piece by piece: tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, and the turban with its gold plate. Anointing oil is also sprinkled on the altar seven times.
2.question: How do outward signs of an office shape the person who wears them?

2.title: The first offerings of the ordination
2.context: Before Aaron offers anything for the people, sacrifices are made for Aaron himself. The priest is a sinner being prepared to serve sinners.
2.question: Why might it matter that a leader's first act is to be dealt with, before dealing with others?

2.title: Blood on ear, thumb, and toe
2.context: Blood from the ordination ram was put on each man's right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe, then oil and blood from the altar were sprinkled on them and their garments.
2.question: Hearing, working, and walking are all marked here. Which of the three most needs marking in your life?

2.title: Seven days at the entrance
2.context: The ordination lasted seven days, spent at the tent entrance under orders not to leave. The length echoes the week of creation: a new order being made.
2.question: What seasons of waiting have prepared you for something you could not have rushed?

2.title: The eighth day
2.context: On the eighth day Aaron offers for himself first, then for the people. Moses tells him the LORD will appear that day.
2.question: What would it mean to approach a long-awaited day knowing you are expected, not merely allowed?

2.title: Fire from the LORD, and the people shout
2.context: When Moses and Aaron come out of the tent and bless the people, the glory of the LORD appears to all the people, and fire consumes the offering. The people shout and fall facedown.
2.question: How do you respond when something you hoped for actually happens in front of you?

2.title: Unauthorized fire
2.context: Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's two oldest sons, offered incense the text calls unauthorized, contrary to God's command. The text does not give their motive, and this retelling does not invent one.
2.question: How do you handle the parts of a hard story where the reasons are simply not given?

2.title: To those who come near Me
2.context: Moses answers the deaths with God's own words about His holiness. Aaron's response recorded in the text is silence.
2.question: When words would be too small for a loss, what does faithful silence look like?

2.title: Carried out, and a rule about wine
2.context: The bodies were carried outside the camp by cousins, still in their tunics. The command against drinking wine when entering the tent is the only instruction in this stretch spoken by God to Aaron directly.
2.question: What boundaries protect the work you do for others from your own worst moments?

2.title: The goat that was burned, not eaten
2.context: Aaron's surviving sons had burned the sin offering goat instead of eating it as commanded. Aaron's answer points to the day itself, and Moses, hearing it, was satisfied.
2.question: When have you had to explain a decision made on the hardest day of your life?

2.title: Two fires in one day
2.context: The priesthood begins with acceptance and judgment on the same day, in the same place, from the same presence. The book treats both fires as one lesson.
2.question: What has a single day taught you that a year of ordinary days could not?

3.title: The table set apart
3.context: The food laws sort land animals, water creatures, birds, and insects by visible marks. The chapter gives its own reason: the God who brought Israel out of Egypt is holy, and His people are to be holy.
3.question: How do ordinary habits, like eating, shape a person's sense of belonging?

3.title: A mother, and the poor mother's birds
3.context: After childbirth a mother brought an offering at the end of her purification days. The law again provides a smaller offering, two birds, for the woman who cannot afford a lamb.
3.question: Where do you see dignity protected by rules that bend toward the poor?

3.title: The priest who waits seven days
3.context: The priest in these chapters is an inspector, not a healer. Again and again his first act is to shut the person up for seven days and look again, rather than pronounce a verdict at once.
3.question: What situations in your life call for a second look before a judgment is made?

3.title: Two birds, and the way back in
3.context: Cleansing used two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop. One bird was killed over fresh water; the living bird, dipped in its blood, was released into the open field.
3.question: What does restoration require beyond being declared clean?

3.title: Houses, discharges, and the reason
3.context: The inspection law even covers mildew in houses in a land Israel has not entered yet. Chapter 15 closes by naming the point: God's dwelling stands among the people.
3.question: How does the nearness of something precious change the way you guard your own life?

3.title: After the death of Aaron's sons
3.context: The Day of Atonement chapter opens by remembering Nadab and Abihu. Aaron is warned not to enter behind the veil freely, or he will die, because God appears in the cloud above the mercy seat.
3.question: How should a previous failure shape the way a person approaches a holy responsibility again?

3.title: Blood behind the veil
3.context: Aaron enters in plain linen rather than the gold of his office, carrying incense whose cloud covers the mercy seat, and blood for himself before blood for the people. Even the tent and altar are cleansed.
3.question: Why might the holiest work require the plainest clothing?

3.title: The goat that carries it away
3.context: Both of Aaron's hands, where other offerings took one, are laid on the living goat while every sin of Israel is confessed over it. The goat is led into a solitary place and released, not killed.
3.question: What is the difference between a sin that is punished and a sin that is carried away?

3.title: Once a year, on the tenth day
3.context: The day is fixed on the tenth day of the seventh month, a Sabbath of complete rest, as a permanent statute. Atonement for the whole nation happens once a year.
3.question: What rhythms of return and repair are built into your year?

3.title: Distinguishing, all the way down
3.context: Five chapters of sorting clean from unclean end at the mercy seat. The next section of the book turns from the camp's purity to the people's daily conduct.
3.question: Where in your life does careful distinguishing protect something you love?

4.title: The life is in the blood
4.context: Slaughter for food was brought to the tent entrance as a peace offering. Blood is barred as food because, the text says, the life of the flesh is in it, and God gave it on the altar for atonement.
4.question: How does treating something as sacred change the way you handle it day to day?

4.title: Not Egypt, not Canaan
4.context: Chapter 18 names the two cultures around Israel and rejects both as patterns. It closes by picturing the land itself vomiting out inhabitants who defile it.
4.question: Which influences around you are you most tempted to copy without noticing?

4.title: Be holy, because I am holy
4.context: Chapter 19 applies holiness to parents, Sabbaths, idols, and the edges of a harvest field, which were left unharvested for the poor and the foreigner. The phrase 'I am the LORD' sounds through the chapter like a refrain.
4.question: What would it change if generosity was treated as a boundary marker of your faith?

4.title: Love your neighbor as yourself
4.context: Wages are not to be held overnight, the deaf are not to be cursed, and nothing is to be placed in a blind person's path. The section rises to the command Jesus later called the second greatest.
4.question: Which of these small protections would make the biggest difference in your workplace?

4.title: The foreigner, and honest scales
4.context: The foreigner living in Israel was to be treated as native-born and loved as oneself, because Israel knew Egypt from the inside. The chapter ends at the market, with honest scales and measures.
4.question: How does remembering your own hardest season change the way you treat an outsider?

4.title: Penalties, and a land that keeps its people
4.context: Chapter 20 repeats much of chapters 18 and 19 with the penalties attached. Its stated aim is that the land Israel is entering will not vomit them out as it did the nations before them.
4.question: Why do you think some instructions only get attention once consequences are named?

4.title: The high priest may not mourn
4.context: Priests were held to a narrower standard around the dead, and the high priest could not take part in mourning even for his father or mother. The rule stands behind Aaron's silence in the episode of the two fires.
4.question: What does your role sometimes require you to carry quietly?

4.title: No defect on the altar
4.context: Offerings had to be without defect to be accepted. Men with defects from Aaron's line still ate the holy food, but did not approach to offer.
4.question: What is the difference between being included and being presented?

4.title: Every corner of the week
4.context: By the end of chapter 22 the law has entered slaughtering, eating, marriage, farming, courts, and markets. What remains unordered is time itself.
4.question: Is there a corner of your week that has not yet been brought under the same care?

5.title: My appointed feasts
5.context: The calendar opens with the weekly Sabbath before any annual feast. Inside the harvest feast itself, the law repeats the command to leave the field's edges for the poor and the foreigner.
5.question: How does a weekly rhythm shape a person differently from an annual event?

5.title: Booths, so your descendants may know
5.context: The seventh month holds trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Tabernacles, when Israel lived in booths for a week after the harvest. The text gives the reason: so later generations would know God made Israel dwell in booths out of Egypt.
5.question: What practices help the next generation remember where a family came from?

5.title: The man who cursed the Name
5.context: The son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father blasphemed the Name during a fight in the camp. He was held in custody until God's decision was known, and the ruling that follows gives one standard of law for foreigner and native alike.
5.question: Why does it matter that the camp waited for a decision instead of settling the case in anger?

5.title: What will we eat in the seventh year?
5.context: Every seventh year the land itself was to rest, with no sowing or pruning. The text raises the obvious objection in the people's own voice and answers it with a promised triple harvest in the sixth year.
5.question: What would it take for you to obey a command whose provision you could not yet see?

5.title: Liberty proclaimed through the land
5.context: After seven Sabbaths of years, the horn sounded on the Day of Atonement and the fiftieth year was consecrated: property returned, debts released their grip, and Israelites who had sold themselves went home with their children.
5.question: What would a built-in fresh start repair in a community over generations?

5.title: I will walk among you
5.context: The blessings move from rain and harvests to peace in the land, and narrow to a promise of presence: God walking among His people as their God, and they His people.
5.question: Which promised good in this list would you find hardest to trust?

5.title: Yet in spite of this
5.context: The warnings escalate in waves, each hinged on refusing to obey after the last. The chapter still does not end in exile: it ends on confession, and on God remembering His covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
5.question: What does it mean that the worst chapter in the book ends with remembrance rather than rejection?

5.title: The last law, and the mountain
5.context: Chapter 27 is a quiet list of vows, valuations, and the tithe passing under the shepherd's rod. The book's final line places everything on Mount Sinai, where Israel has been camped all along.
5.question: Looking back over Leviticus, which single image will stay with you: the fire, the goat, the booths, or the fiftieth year?
